questions.title: Pumping lemma
questions.question: Which quantifier order describes the pumping lemma for a regular L?

options.label: For every split there exists p making all words pumpable.
For every p there exists a split of every word outside L.
There exists one word and one k proving regularity.
There exists p; for every long enough w∈L there exists a legal split; for every k≥0 the pumped word stays in L.

questions.explanation: The split may depend on w, and p depends on L. The universal pumping claim applies to all k for that chosen split.

questions.title: Pumping lemma
questions.question: Which conditions must a legal split w=xyz satisfy?
questions.explanation: y must be nonempty and must end within the first p symbols. x and z may be empty, and w is at least p symbols long.

questions.title: Pumping lemma
questions.question: What is xy^0z?
questions.explanation: Pumping with k=0 deletes y only. k=1 restores the original word and cannot create a contradiction for w∈L.

questions.title: Pumping lemma
questions.question: In a nonregularity proof, who effectively determines the legal split?

options.label: The proof must work for every legal split, not just a convenient one.
The split must always have x=ε and |y|=1.
The input alphabet uniquely fixes it.
The prover may choose one arbitrary split and ignore the others.

questions.explanation: Negating the lemma requires defeating every allowed decomposition of the chosen witness. A bad single split can occur even in a regular language.

questions.title: Pumping lemma
questions.question: For L={0^n1^n:n≥0} and w=0^p1^p, what must y look like in every legal split?
questions.explanation: |xy|≤p keeps the pumping segment inside the initial zero block; |y|>0 supplies a positive d.

questions.title: Pumping lemma
questions.question: For L={0^n1^n:n≥0}, take witness w=0^p1^p and any legal split w=xyz with y=0^d, 1≤d≤p. What happens at k=2?

options.label: It must remain in L because d≤p.
The word has p+d zeros and p ones, so it is outside L.
The word has p zeros and p+d ones.

questions.explanation: Only y repeats; z's ones are unchanged. Unequal counts contradict the required language membership.

questions.title: Pumping lemma
questions.question: For L={a^i b^j:i<j}, use w=a^p b^(p+1). Why does k=2 work for every legal y=a^d?

options.label: p+d is always less than p+1.
p+d≥p+1, so the strict inequality fails.
The number of b symbols becomes p.
d can be chosen to be zero.

questions.explanation: Since d≥1, the new a count is at least the b count. Equality already violates i<j.

questions.title: Pumping lemma
questions.question: If a language satisfies the pumping condition, can that alone prove it regular?

options.label: Yes, if the alphabet is finite.
Yes; the converse is part of the lemma.
Only if ε is absent, then yes.
No; the lemma gives a necessary condition, not an equivalence.

questions.explanation: The implication is regular ⇒ pumpable. A separate representation or theorem is needed to prove regularity.

questions.title: Pumping lemma
questions.question: How can a finite language satisfy the lemma?

options.label: Every word must contain a nonempty loop.
Finite languages are exceptions to the lemma.
Choose p larger than every word length, leaving no eligible witness to check.

questions.explanation: The quantified statement is then vacuously true. Empty language also satisfies it for any positive p.

questions.title: Pumping lemma
questions.question: Why does a DFA with N states support a pumping bound p=N?

options.label: Every accepted word has length N.
Its first N transitions visit N+1 states counting the initial visit, so some state repeats.
Every loop contains exactly N symbols.

questions.explanation: The repeated-state segment consumes a nonempty y within the first N symbols. Repeating or omitting this loop preserves the final destination. Larger bounds such as N+1 also work.

questions.title: Count fixed-length words
questions.question: A code has 2 letter positions followed by 2 digit positions. Each letter position independently has 26 choices and each digit position independently has 10 choices. Repetition is allowed and every choice is a single symbol. Prove finiteness and calculate the exact number of words.
questions.explanation: The positions are fixed in number. Choices multiply across independent positions; allowing repeated symbols does not allow unlimited length.
worked_solution: There are 26^2 letter prefixes and 10^2 digit suffixes.
The total is 26^2 × 10^2 = 67,600. Every code has length 4, so the set is finite.

questions.title: Reason about repeated blocks
questions.question: Analyze L((110*)*). Derive a structural invariant, test ε and the shortest nonempty all-1 word, and select the correct conclusion. A maximal run is the entire uninterrupted block of 1s.

options.label: Every word contains at least one 0; maximal 1-runs have exactly 2 symbols.
Every maximal 1-run has length divisible by 2; ε and 11 belong.
Every word has total length divisible by 2; ε is excluded.
The substring 111 never occurs, even inside longer runs.

questions.explanation: Each factor contributes 2 consecutive 1s. Zero-length zero blocks allow adjacent factors to merge, so a maximal run can contain any positive multiple of 2 ones.
worked_solution: Zero outer repetitions give ε. One factor with zero zero-block repetitions gives 11.
If k adjacent factors meet without zeros, their 1-run has length 2k. A positive zero block ends a run; it never changes the number of 1s already in it.
Two factors with no zeros produce 1111, which contains the shorter substring 111. Substring occurrence is not the same as maximal-run length.

questions.title: Construct an endpoint language
questions.question: Over Σ={0,1}, construct the language of nonempty words whose first symbol is 0 and last symbol is 0. A one-symbol word is allowed if it satisfies both conditions. Which expression is exact?
questions.explanation: The construction in the worked solution preserves exactly the required words.
worked_solution: Begin with singleton symbol languages and form Σ by union. Then Σ* is regular by star.
The length-at-least-two portion is 0(0|1)*0; it uses concatenation of regular languages.
Add 0 as a singleton alternative.
Every constructed word has the required endpoints; conversely, every eligible longer word has some middle word in Σ*. Thus the expression is exact and the language is regular.

option_feedback.A: Counterexample ε: target rejects, but this expression accepts.
option_feedback.B: Counterexample 0: target accepts, but this expression rejects.
option_feedback.C: This expression describes exactly the target language.
option_feedback.D: Counterexample 01: target rejects, but this expression accepts.

questions.question: Construct, using regular operations, the words over {0,1} whose number of 0 symbols is congruent to 1 modulo 2. Occurrences of 1 may appear anywhere. Choose an exact expression.

Use 1 copies of B, followed by zero or more groups of 2 copies. The count is 1+2k, k≥0.

questions.title: Use closure for length restrictions
questions.question: Let D be the language of single decimal digits. Consider digit strings whose length is divisible by 2 or 5, but not by 10. Leading zeros are allowed. Give a regularity proof without the pumping lemma.

options.label: Nonregular: the language has infinitely many lengths.

questions.explanation: Star constructs multiples of each block length, union represents OR, and difference removes the excluded multiples.
worked_solution: D is finite, so it is regular. Fixed powers are repeated concatenations.
The target is ((D^2)* ∪ (D^5)*) \ (D^10)*, regular by closure.
As a check, allowed residues modulo 10 are [2, 4, 5, 6, 8]. Length zero is excluded because it is divisible by 10.

questions.title: Isolate prime lengths
questions.question: Let P={a^p:p is prime}, known nonregular, and E=(aa)*. Classify E∪P without the pumping lemma and identify a useful regular intersection filter.

options.label: Nonregular; intersect with E to obtain P.
Regular; a union is regular regardless of its inputs.
Regular; P contains only finite words.

questions.explanation: All primes except 2 are odd. The regular filter keeps every prime and removes every nonprime even length.
worked_solution: Assume E∪P is regular. Let H=(aa)*a | aa, regular by an expression.
(E∪P)∩H=P: length 2 is retained, odd prime lengths are retained, and all other even lengths are removed.
Intersection closure would make P regular, contradicting the given fact. Therefore the union is nonregular.

questions.title: A nonregular ingredient can yield a regular result
questions.question: Let Σ={0,1} and K={0^n1^n:n≥1}. Simplify Σ*KΣ* and select its exact regex. Then justify regularity without the pumping lemma.
questions.explanation: The construction in the worked solution preserves exactly the required words.
worked_solution: Every central block 0^n1^n contains the adjacent pair 01; thus Σ*KΣ* is contained in the language containing 01.
Conversely, if a word contains 01, choose n=1 and absorb the surrounding symbols into the two Σ* portions.
The languages are equal. The displayed regex proves the result regular, despite K being nonregular.

option_feedback.A: Counterexample 001: target accepts, but this expression rejects.
option_feedback.B: Counterexample ε: target rejects, but this expression accepts.
option_feedback.C: Counterexample 01: target accepts, but this expression rejects.
option_feedback.D: This expression describes exactly the target language.

questions.explanation: Intersecting an assumed-regular L with the regular block-pattern language isolates a known nonregular count comparison.
worked_solution: Assume L regular. The filter a*c* is regular by its regex.

questions.title: Design a DFA for endpoint conditions
questions.question: Construct a complete DFA over {0,1} for nonempty words with equal first and last symbols. Use S for no symbols read and a two-symbol state uv to mean first symbol u, last symbol v. One-symbol words are eligible when they satisfy the condition. Which final-state set is correct?
questions.explanation: The state records both endpoints seen so far. Reading a new symbol changes only the remembered last symbol.
worked_solution: Start at S, which is nonfinal because the empty word has no endpoints. The first symbol c moves to cc.
From uv, input c moves to uc. Mark final precisely those endpoint pairs satisfying the requested condition.
This invariant proves both acceptance of all eligible words and rejection of every other word.

questions.title: Design a suffix DFA with overlaps
questions.question: Construct a complete DFA for words over {0,1} ending in 010. State qj records the length j of the longest suffix that is a prefix of 010. Which row gives the destinations from q2 on inputs 0 and 1, in that order?
questions.explanation: After appending a symbol, retain the longest suffix that remains a prefix of the target pattern; do not blindly reset on every mismatch.
worked_solution: The start is q0 and the sole final state is q3. A final state still has outgoing transitions because extra input can destroy or restore the suffix.
From q2, append each input to the remembered prefix 01. The longest valid suffix lengths are [3, 0].

questions.title: Design a DFA for nonoverlapping prefix and suffix
questions.question: Construct a complete DFA for the regex 10(0|1)*01. The fixed prefix and suffix occupy separate positions, so words have length at least four. Which word is accepted?
questions.explanation: The middle star may contribute ε, giving 1001. It does not permit the required prefix and suffix to overlap.
worked_solution: P0 and P1 verify the fixed prefix 10; a mismatch enters X. After consuming the prefix, enter T0.
Tj remembers the matched prefix length of the suffix 01 within the remaining input. Only T2 is final.
The shortest accepted word is 1001. This proves that a mere overlapping start/end occurrence is insufficient for this regex.

questions.title: Complement a complete DFA
questions.question: Construct a complete DFA over {0,1} for words NOT matching 00(0|1)*10. Use prefix states P0,P1, tail states T0,T1,T2, and rejecting-error state X of the original positive-language DFA. Which final set should the complemented DFA have?
questions.explanation: First complete the positive-language DFA, then swap final and nonfinal membership for every state. Its old rejecting sink must become accepting too.
worked_solution: The positive-language DFA has only T2 final. Its complete state set is {P0,P1,T0,T1,T2,X}.
The complement uses all states except T2 as finals: {P0,P1,T0,T1,X}. It includes ε and words too short to match the original regex.
